At first, this may seem like a problem that comes with success. More orders mean more work, and more work naturally requires additional effort. But when delays, repeated follow-ups and coordination problems become part of the daily routine, the issue may be more than simply having too much work. As a business expands, its processes, responsibilities and management systems need to keep pace with the additional complexity. The challenge is not just handling a larger workload. It is ensuring that the organisation can manage that workload without losing control over costs, quality and delivery commitments. Growth Can Put Pressure on Existing Processes Consider a manufacturing business that initially handles a manageable number of customer orders each week. Its sales team communicates directly with production, purchasing knows which materials are required, and managers can resolve most issues through quick discussions. As the business grows, the number of orders increases and several customers begin requesting different products and delivery schedules. The same informal approach becomes harder to maintain. Production receives frequent changes to its schedule, purchasing struggles to keep up with updated material requirements, and the sales team spends more time checking order status. Employees may continue working hard, but the additional coordination starts consuming time that could otherwise be spent completing orders. A useful response is to examine whether the existing processes are still suitable for the current scale of the business. Clearer order tracking, better production planning and agreed procedures for handling changes can help reduce unnecessary disruption. More Employees Do Not Automatically Mean Better Coordination When a company expands, hiring additional employees is often necessary. However, increasing the size of a team does not automatically improve the way work moves between departments. For example, a growing distribution business may hire more sales representatives to handle customer demand. The larger sales team generates more orders, but the warehouse and purchasing departments continue operating with their previous planning methods. As a result, orders may be accepted before stock availability is confirmed, warehouse employees receive incomplete information, and customers need to follow up about delivery dates. The problem is not necessarily a shortage of employees. It may be a mismatch between the way departments work and the volume of business they now handle. Before adding more resources, management should understand where the workflow becomes difficult to manage. Better communication, clearer responsibilities and improved information sharing may resolve some problems without creating additional layers of work. Identify Where Decisions and Work Get Delayed Operational delays are not always caused by machines, employees or a lack of resources. Sometimes, work stops because nobody knows who should make the next decision. A purchase request may wait for approval even when it falls within an established budget. A customer issue may pass between departments because responsibility has not been clearly assigned. A production change may remain pending while several managers wait for information from one another. These delays can be difficult to recognise when each department looks only at its own activities. Management can begin by reviewing recurring problems and asking a few practical questions: Where do employees regularly wait for information or approval? Which tasks require repeated follow-ups before they can be completed? Are responsibilities clear when a problem involves multiple departments? Which routine decisions could be handled without senior management intervention? Are delays being recorded and reviewed, or are employees simply working around them? The answers can help leaders identify where the organisation needs clearer decision-making processes rather than more activity. Why Operational Improvement Requires a Wider View A change that benefits one department may create difficulties somewhere else if the wider process is not considered. For instance, purchasing may place larger orders to obtain lower material prices. Although the purchase cost per unit decreases, the additional stock occupies warehouse space and ties up money that the business may need for other expenses. Similarly, sales may offer a shorter delivery time to win a customer, but production may need overtime or urgent material purchases to fulfil the commitment. Each decision may appear reasonable when viewed separately. The wider impact becomes visible only when purchasing, finance, sales and operations consider how their decisions affect one another. This is why business improvement should look beyond isolated departmental targets. Leaders need to understand how work flows through the organisation, where resources are being used and which decisions create unnecessary costs or delays. A more connected approach allows businesses to prioritise improvements that support overall performance rather than solving one problem while creating another.
